drills.title: Leased, physical, and economic occupancy
drills.question: An office building has 200,000 rsf. Leases cover 180,000 sf. One 10,000 sf tenant has moved out but still pays rent. Tenants on another 20,000 sf (moved in) are in a free-rent period. All leases carry the same rent per sf. Give leased, physical, and economic occupancy.
drills.solution: Leased = 180,000/200,000 = 90%. Physical excludes the dark suite: 170,000/200,000 = 85%. Economic excludes space not paying: (180,000 - 20,000)/200,000 = 80% (the dark tenant pays, so it counts economically).
common_mistakes: Reporting leased occupancy as 'occupancy' in a valuation
Excluding the dark tenant from economic occupancy (it pays) or including the free-rent tenants (they do not)
drills.intuition: Three questions: who has signed, who is in the building, who is paying. Each answers a different risk.
drills.takeaway: Dark space is future vacancy with a date; free-rent space is a concession already granted. Underwrite both explicitly.

drills.title: Loaded cap rate and the seller's tax bill
drills.question: Pre-tax NOI is $1,200,000. Market cap rate on NOI after reassessed tax is 7.0%. Tax is 2.5% of value and resets to the price. The seller's current tax bill is $150,000. Give the value and the overpayment of a buyer who capitalizes NOI after the seller's bill.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing the seller's tax bill
Adding the tax rate to the cap rate when tax will not be reassessed (e.g., a refinance)
drills.intuition: When tax depends on price, value and tax are solved together: V = N/(c+t).
drills.takeaway: The larger the gap between the old assessment and your price, the larger the error from ignoring reassessment.

drills.title: Months of supply
drills.question: A submarket has 2.4 million sf vacant and 3.0 million sf under construction, 40% pre-leased. Net absorption runs 350,000 sf a month. How many months of supply?
drills.solution: Speculative pipeline = 3.0 x 0.60 = 1.8m sf. MOS = (2.4 + 1.8)/0.35 = 12.0 months.
common_mistakes: Counting pre-leased space as supply
Using quarterly or annual absorption without converting to monthly
drills.intuition: Supply measured in months of demand puts vacancy and pipeline on one scale.
drills.takeaway: Ask whether pre-leasing tenants are relocating within the same submarket; if so, their move-outs add supply.

drills.title: Positive absorption, rising vacancy
drills.question: A quarterly report shows positive net absorption for the third straight quarter, yet the vacancy rate rose each quarter. A colleague calls the report contradictory. Explain how both can be true, and what you would check.

rubric: Completions exceeded absorption: vacancy identity V' = V + C - AB, so positive AB with larger C raises vacancy
Inventory growth: deliveries enlarge the denominator, but vacant new space raises the numerator faster
Checks the pipeline delivered in the quarter and how much was pre-leased
Checks whether pre-leasing tenants vacated space in the same submarket (backfill risk, sublease additions)
Notes possible definitional differences (direct vs total vacancy including sublease; inventory changes from reclassification)

drills.solution: Nothing is contradictory. Vacant space rises whenever completions exceed net absorption. Check completions, pre-leasing, sublease availability, and any inventory reclassification.
common_mistakes: Treating positive absorption as proof of a tightening market
Ignoring sublease space
drills.intuition: Absorption is demand; vacancy is demand relative to supply.
drills.takeaway: Read absorption next to completions every time.

drills.title: Operating leverage meets financial leverage
drills.question: A full-service hotel has $10.0m revenue, fixed costs $5.5m, and variable costs 20% of revenue. Revenue falls 10%. Cap rate is unchanged at 8.5%. Debt is 60% of the starting value. Give base NOI, the NOI change, and the equity change. Would you finance this asset at 60% LTV? State conditions.

rubric: Computes DOL = 8.0/2.5 = 3.2 and links it to the NOI change
Recognizes that cap rates usually widen in hotel downturns, so -80% is not the worst case
Ties LTV to a stress that includes both revenue and cap-rate moves; proposes lower leverage or reserves
States what would change the answer (cost flexibility, management contract terms, debt structure)

drills.solution: NOI = 10.0 x 0.8 - 5.5 = $2.5m. After -10%: 9.0 x 0.8 - 5.5 = $1.7m, -32%. DOL = 8.0/2.5 = 3.2. Value falls 32%; equity at 60% LTV falls 32%/0.4 = 80%. 60% LTV is too high for this cost structure unless there are debt-service reserves and a stress that includes cap-rate widening still shows positive equity.
common_mistakes: Assuming NOI falls 10% because revenue fell 10%
Ignoring cap-rate widening in the stress
drills.intuition: Operating leverage and financial leverage multiply.
drills.takeaway: Size debt on the product of DOL and LTV, not on either alone.

drills.title: Apartment NOI from market rent
drills.question: A 120-unit apartment property: average market rent $1,450/month. Deductions from gross potential rent: loss-to-lease 3%, vacancy 6%, concessions 1%, bad debt 1.5%. Other income $90 per unit per month. Operating expenses $6,200 per unit per year before management; management 3% of EGI. Reserve $300 per unit per year. Compute GPR, EGI, NOI, and NCF.
common_mistakes: Applying vacancy to EGI after other income
Forgetting loss-to-lease (in-place rents below market)
Deducting the reserve and calling the result NOI
drills.intuition: Start from market rent and walk down to cash; each deduction is a separate risk.
drills.takeaway: Loss-to-lease is upside only if leases can roll to market; concessions are a cost even when called 'marketing'.

drills.title: Deferred maintenance: price, not cap rate
drills.question: Seller NOI (no reserve) is $2.0m. Market reserve $100,000 a year. Cap rate 6.5% on NOI after reserve. The PCA shows $900,000 of immediate repairs; use a 10% contingency. What price, and how far below the seller's ask at 6.5% on its NOI?
common_mistakes: Capitalizing the one-time repair at the cap rate
Omitting the reserve because the PCA 'already covers' capex
drills.intuition: Permanent items go through the cap rate; one-time items come off in dollars.
drills.takeaway: Negotiate one-time items as credits or escrows, permanent items as price.

drills.title: The T-12 and the rent roll disagree

inputs.seller_explanation: expense savings and a one-time recovery

drills.question: A seller's T-12 shows NOI up 30% year over year on a multi-tenant office building. The rent roll shows occupancy down 6 points over the same period. The broker says the increase came from 'expense savings and a one-time recovery' and wants bids in 48 hours. You have no general ledger, bank statements, or tax bills. What do you do?

rubric: Identifies the contradiction: lower occupancy with higher NOI requires either non-recurring income, deferred expenses, or an error
Removes the one-time recovery and tests whether 'savings' are deferred maintenance or unpaid taxes
Lists the documents that would reconcile the two (GL, bank deposits vs rent roll, tax bills, AP aging)
Abstains from a firm bid in 48 hours; at most submits a non-binding indication priced on the prior year's NOI less the occupancy loss, conditional on reconciliation
States that passing is acceptable if the seller will not provide reconciling documents

drills.solution: Abstain from a firm bid. Price only on information that reconciles. A non-binding indication on the prior-year NOI adjusted for lost occupancy, conditioned on the GL and bank statements, is the most that is defensible.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing the T-12 because it is 'actual'
Treating a broker's verbal explanation as evidence
drills.intuition: When two seller documents disagree, the one closer to cash (bank deposits) wins; the one closer to marketing loses.
drills.takeaway: Abstention is a decision. A missed deal costs nothing; a capitalized error costs the cap-rate multiple.

drills.title: WALT with and without the largest tenant
drills.question: Three tenants pay $600,000 (7.0 years left), $300,000 (2.0 years), and $100,000 (0.5 years). Compute WALT by rent, and WALT excluding the largest tenant.
common_mistakes: Averaging terms without weights (3.17 years)
Reporting only the portfolio WALT
drills.intuition: WALT hides concentration; strip out the anchor to see the rest of the building.
drills.takeaway: A five-year WALT can be a seven-year lease and a short-term problem.

drills.title: Proposition 13 base year and comparable cap rates
drills.question: A long-held California building has pre-tax NOI of $3.0m. The seller's tax bill is $80,000 on an old base-year value. The buyer's tax will be 1.1% of the price (1% levy plus local debt). The market cap rate on NOI after reassessed tax is 5.0%. Give the value with reassessment, the value a buyer would compute on the seller's NOI, and the overpayment. Then explain how this affects the comparable-sales cap rates you collect.

rubric: Uses V = N/(c + t) with the base year reset to the price
Explains that Proposition 13 resets the base year on change in ownership, so the seller's low tax bill does not transfer
Recomputes comparable cap rates on buyers' reassessed taxes before using them
Notes the 2% annual inflation cap on base-year growth benefits the holder, not the next buyer

drills.solution: V = 3,000,000/(0.05 + 0.011) = $49,180,328. Wrong: (3,000,000 - 80,000)/0.05 = $58,400,000. Overpayment $9,219,672 (18.7%). Comparable cap rates computed on sellers' NOIs overstate yields available to buyers; restate them on reassessed tax.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing the seller's tax bill
Assuming Proposition 13 means no reassessment on sale
drills.intuition: Acquisition-value regimes reset at the sale; the holder's benefit is not for sale.
drills.takeaway: Compare loaded cap rates (c + t), not headline cap rates, across tax regimes.
